newsitem.title: CROATIA: US envoy says Croatia's E.Slavonia poll was fair.
newsitem.headline: US envoy says Croatia's E.Slavonia poll was fair.

text.p: U.S. ambassador Peter Galbraith said on Monday that elections in the former rebel Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia were fair despite disruptions and that most Serbs who wanted to vote cast ballots.

Croatia held municipal and county elections on Sunday and former rebel Serbs took part for the first time. But voting in Eastern Slavonia was extended for a day after complaints that polling stations opened late and registration lists were incomplete.
"The overwhelming majority who could vote in fact did vote," Galbraith told reporters in Vukovar. "Nobody could say that these were perfect elections, but they were fair elections."
Between 85 and 90 percent of those eligible to vote did so, according to U.N. officials.

Analysts say at least a quarter of the enclave's 150,000 Serbs will probably flee to Serbia after the elections, fearing Croatian President Franjo Tudjman's security guarantees will not restrain vengeful Croat war refugees who will soon return to reclaim their homes.
Croatia rejected U.N. charges that its poor planning disrupted the first day of voting.

"UNTAES (U.N. Transitional Authority) is very disappointed with the inadequate and incomplete support of the Croatian side in these elections," mission spokesman Philip Arnold told a news conference in the enclave's main town, Vukovar.
"We were deeply disappointed with the administrative breakdown yesterday -- the fact that packages of ballots were misdirected and voting lists were not corrected," Arnold said.
Croatian officials dismissed the charges, quoting unforeseeable circumstances including the fact that the number of voters was still unknown on the eve of the polls.
"We are rejecting such accusations. I think we have done everything within our power to make sure the election goes all right," an official of the state election commission in Zagreb told Reuters.

"We had no way of knowing what electoral body we were facing in Eastern Slavonia. According to our information, people there were registering to vote as late as Saturday evening," the official, who asked not to be named, said.

The administrator of the enclave, U.S. General Jacques Klein, had previously blamed the delays in voter registration on hardline Serb leaders who dissuaded the people from taking Croatian documents, which would qualify them to vote.
But the Croatian official said UNTAES was also to blame.

"Even if ballot forms were misplaced, the area is small and every polling station did receive a number of forms. UNTAES could have gone ahead with the voting on Sunday and contacted us in the process to put things right," she said.
Faced with a possible collapse of the polls on Sunday, UNTAES eventually allowed any Serb who had obtained a Croatian state identity card to vote even if their name was not on voter lists.
Zagreb hurriedly despatched an extra 110,000 ballots to the enclave on Monday morning, which were then "speeded around the enclave", Arnold said.
"Today, with the additional people voting, we think that an overwhelming majority of voters will be able to take part in the elections," he said.
UNTAES's mandate expires in July and Croatia's nationalist authorities are strongly opposed to any extension.
